key_insight: A Bayesian finite-element model reconstructs steady blood-flow velocity and pressure from sparse noisy measurements while quantifying uncertainty.
engineering_relevance: It enables clinically useful, physics-consistent flow estimates and uncertainty bounds for metrics such as pressure drop, flow rate, and wall shear stress without requiring offline training data.
method: Taylor-Hood finite elements represent velocity and pressure fields.
Physics-informed maximum-entropy priors and a noise-based likelihood define the posterior.
MAP inference is solved as a sparse nonlinear least-squares problem; a Laplace approximation propagates uncertainty to quantities of interest.
evidence_signal: The method was evaluated on patient-specific cerebral aneurysm, aortic aneurysm, and aortic coarctation geometries, where it outperformed tricubic interpolation and matched a PINN for field reconstruction while improving wall shear stress estimates.
watch_item: Performance depends on the assumed noise model and the accuracy of the Laplace approximation, so uncertainty estimates may be less reliable when measurements are highly non-Gaussian or strongly sparse.
paper_title: Bayesian finite element regression for vascular flow reconstruction with quantified uncertainty
